label: Parametric Models on Spheres and Shapes
notes: This appendix on printed pages 225 to 228 collects the classical parametric densities that serve as kernels and benchmarks throughout the book. On the sphere we meet von Mises-Fisher, Bingham, and Watson; on the planar shape space we meet their complex analogues, all built from quadratic or linear exponents.

label: Why Parametric Baselines
notes: Before trusting nonparametric estimators we need parametric yardsticks. These densities are simple, identifiable, and have computable normalizing constants, so they calibrate the flexible mixture methods. They also act as mixture kernels: each nonparametric Bayes model is a countable blend of these very same unimodal building blocks.

label: The von Mises-Fisher Distribution
notes: The von Mises-Fisher law is the sphere's Gaussian analogue. Its log density is linear in the observation through the mean direction mu, so the distribution is unimodal and rotationally symmetric about mu. The concentration kappa controls spread: large kappa tightens the cloud, kappa zero gives the uniform law.

label: vMF Concentration and Contours
notes: As kappa grows the density contours collapse toward the mean direction mu, mirroring how a Gaussian sharpens as variance shrinks. The diagram shows nested level sets tightening around mu while the antipode stays a minimum. This intuition explains why kappa is read as an inverse-variance concentration parameter on the sphere.

label: The Bingham Distribution
notes: The Bingham density uses a quadratic exponent x-transpose A x, so replacing x by its antipode leaves it unchanged. This antipodal symmetry makes it a model for axes rather than directions, a law on real projective space. The symmetric matrix A encodes both the principal axis and the anisotropy of the spread.

label: The Watson Distribution
notes: The Watson law is the rotationally symmetric special case of Bingham, where A is rank-one up to a scalar. A single concentration parameter governs whether mass clusters around an axis, a girdle, or spreads uniformly. It is the simplest axial model and the natural one-parameter benchmark for symmetric axial data.

label: Direction Versus Axis
notes: The key contrast is symmetry. A directional model like von Mises-Fisher distinguishes x from minus x and concentrates at one pole. An axial model like Bingham or Watson identifies x with minus x, so its density is symmetric across the equatorial plane and lives naturally on projective space, not the sphere.

label: Planar Shapes as CP^{k-2}
notes: Kendall's planar shape space Sigma-k-2 is the complex projective space CP to the k minus two. Landmark configurations become unit complex vectors on the pre-shape sphere, and rotation and scaling quotient out as multiplication by a unit complex scalar. Parametric models must respect this complex projective invariance to be well defined.

label: Complex Bingham and Complex Watson
notes: On the planar shape space the Bingham and Watson laws reappear with a Hermitian quadratic form z-star A z. Because A is Hermitian the density is invariant under the unit-scalar phase, so it descends to CP. The complex Watson is the unimodal rank-one case used as the primary kernel for planar shapes.

label: Normalizing Constants and MLEs
notes: Each density needs a normalizing constant: confluent hypergeometric functions for vMF and Watson, eigenvalue-dependent constants for Bingham. Maximum likelihood sends the mean direction to the resultant vector and the concentration to a solved ratio of those normalizers, while axial models read the mean axis from the dominant eigenvector of the scatter.

label: Kernels for Nonparametric Bayes
notes: These parametric laws are the kernels of the book's nonparametric Bayes mixtures. A Dirichlet process places a prior over countably many vMF, Watson, or complex Watson components, blending unimodal benchmarks into flexible densities. Understanding each kernel's invariance and concentration is what keeps the resulting mixture honest on its manifold.
